title: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the days on Vaishnava theology, reading the Brahma Sutra with Ramanuja: a world made from fullness, as play.
screen: `VAISHNAVA THEOLOGY: RAMANUJA'S READING.` · `A WEEK TO LOOK BACK ON.`

segments.voice: Late afternoon on a beach. Something flashes in the wet sand, and a kid runs for it, shouting that it's silver. It isn't. It's the inside of a shell, catching the light. For a few seconds, though, the silver was completely real to that kid. The running was real. The shout was real. Nothing in the sand changed when the mistake was seen. Only the seeing changed. That little scene is a Vedanta teaching example, and Shankara reaches for it before he has commented on a single line of the Brahma Sutra. Last week was the Brahma Sutra with Ramanuja. Now its opening pages, with Shankara, and his word: jnana.
screen: `SILVER IN THE SAND.` → `IT WAS A SHELL.` → `ONLY THE SEEING CHANGED.`

segments.voice: Jnana means knowing, knowledge. In this tradition it also names a whole way: freedom that comes through knowing, rather than through doing more. Shankara's commentary opens with a preface before the first sutra. He sets two things side by side: the one who knows, the I, and everything that can be known, the this. They are as opposed, he says, as darkness and light. Neither can be the other. And yet everyone mixes them up, all the time, without trying. I am tall. I am tired. I am going. This is mine. The knower takes on the features of the known, and the known borrows the life of the knower. He calls the mix-up adhyasa, placing one thing on another, like silver placed on shell, or one moon seen as two by a tired eye. Then something bold: ordinary life runs on this mix-up. Everyday ways of knowing, even the rules for ritual action, all work inside it. He isn't mocking daily life; he's describing where it stands. And the Upanishads, he says, are studied to undo the mix-up, not by adding a new experience, but by knowing. That knowing is jnana. Not every Vedanta teacher accepts this preface. Ramanuja argues against it at length in his own commentary, and his followers read the same sutras another way. For the next few days, Shankara makes his case through the first four lines.
screen: `JNANA: FREEDOM THROUGH KNOWING.` · `THE I AND THE THIS.` · `ADHYASA: SILVER ON THE SHELL.` · `THE TEXTS STUDIED TO UNDO IT.`

segments.voice: Notice one sensation, maybe tiredness, maybe warmth in the hands, and hear the sentence the mind makes about it: I am tired. Then, gently, say it another way inside: tiredness is being noticed. Don't argue with either sentence; just feel the small difference between them, and if you pray, rest in that noticing as your prayer.
Jnana. Knowing, and the way of freedom through knowing. For Shankara, the knowing that undoes the mix-up of the I and the this.
Your line: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening, Shankara's commentary, one point one point one to one point one point four. Nothing in the sand changed; only the seeing did. See you tomorrow.

chat.says: Shankara says people mix up the I and the this. What does he mean?
options: The knower takes on the features of the known, like silver seen on a shell.
He means people forget their own names when they're tired or stressed.
He means grammar: 'I' and 'this' get swapped in careless Sanskrit sentences.
chat.meaning: Shankara's preface calls it adhyasa: the I and the this, opposed as darkness and light, placed on each other like silver on shell.
